text:
Corn root and stem growth are closely linked and continue throughout much of the plant's life. Good soil structure and moisture are important throughout the season, not just at planting, both to support this ongoing root development and to reduce the risk of the plant lodging (falling over) later in the season when it is tall and carrying a heavy ear.

The root system develops in stages: temporary seminal roots from the seed are followed by permanent nodal (crown) roots from the lower stem, which do most of the water and nutrient uptake; brace (prop) roots emerging from above-ground nodes near the base add support once the plant is tall. Root hairs can reach a working depth of roughly 16-28 cm in good soil conditions, and soil compaction, poor drainage, or drought all restrict this development and therefore limit yield potential.

The stem is made up of a series of nodes and internodes; leaves, buds and (near the base) roots arise from the nodes. Final plant height and the number of nodes vary with variety and growing conditions -- see the variety characteristics table for typical height ranges by variety.
